# 大乘破有論

**ID:** T1574
**Volume:** T30
**Category:** 中觀部類
**Original Category:** 中觀部
**Byline:** 龍樹菩薩造  宋 施護譯
**Dynasty:** 宋
**Date:** 980
**Juans:** 1
**CBETA:** https://cbetaonline.dila.edu.tw/zh/T1574

## Contributors
- 龍樹 (A001482)
- 施護 (A000844)

## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

A short Mādhyamaka treatise in one fascicle attributed to Nāgārjuna, translated at Biànjīng 汴京 by [施護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%96%BD%E8%AD%B7) Dānapāla 施護 (Shīhù, *Sahasrabhuja*, North-Indian Mahāyāna translator at the Northern-Song imperial *yìjīngyuán* 譯經院 from c. 980 onward). The translation falls within Dānapāla's main translation phase 982–1000. The Indic original is conventionally identified as a *Bhavasaṃkrāntiśāstra* "Treatise on the Transmission of Becoming" or related Mādhyamaka *prakaraṇa*; the Tibetan tradition preserves a closely parallel work as *Srid pa 'pho ba'i mdo* (Tōh. 226).

**Abstract**

The treatise opens: "I take refuge in all Buddhas. Those who possess wisdom should know all *dharmas* truly. What does this mean? It means: all natures arise from no-nature, and not from no-nature either. If natures had genuine arising, they would be permanent. The intrinsic nature is unreal — like a sky-flower. Know that all *dharmas* are equal to space; their arising is also equal to space; all *pratyaya*-conditioned *dharmas* are equal to space; lacking reality, how could they have being?" 歸命一切佛諸有智者應當如實了知諸法。此中云何。謂一切性從無性生。亦非無性生…… The opening establishes the work's doctrinal programme as Mādhyamaka *prakaraṇa* refuting the substantialist conception of *bhāva* (有 "existence / nature").

The work is doctrinally close to the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā* and the *Śūnyatāsaptati* of the Nāgārjuna corpus, both of which were also translated by [施護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%96%BD%E8%AD%B7) in the same Biànjīng *yìjīngyuán* phase ([KR6m0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6m/KR6m0020) T1575 and [KR6m0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6m/KR6m0021) T1576). T1574, T1575, and T1576 together represent the largest single-translator contribution to the Indic Mādhyamaka short-treatise corpus in Chinese, and are the only Chinese witnesses to several key works of the Nāgārjuna corpus that are otherwise preserved only in Tibetan.
